title: Word: meticulous
body: Meaning: showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise.
example_sentence: She kept meticulous records of every test.

title: Word: ubiquitous
body: Meaning: present, appearing or found everywhere.
example_sentence: Mobile phones have become ubiquitous in every city.

title: Word: pragmatic
body: Meaning: dealing with things in a practical, realistic way rather than by theory.
example_sentence: We need a pragmatic solution we can start this week.

title: Word: ambiguous
body: Meaning: open to more than one interpretation; not clear.
example_sentence: The contract's wording was ambiguous, so both sides disagreed.

title: Word: eloquent
body: Meaning: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing.
example_sentence: Her eloquent speech moved the whole audience.

title: Word: resilient
body: Meaning: able to recover quickly from difficulties.
example_sentence: Small businesses proved resilient during the crisis.

title: Word: candid
body: Meaning: truthful and straightforward; frank.
example_sentence: Thank you for your candid feedback on my report.

title: Word: succinct
body: Meaning: briefly and clearly expressed.
example_sentence: Keep your answer succinct: two sentences at most.

title: Word: scrutinise
body: Meaning: to examine or inspect closely and thoroughly. Also spelled 'scrutinize'.
example_sentence: The committee will scrutinise the budget line by line.

title: Word: mitigate
body: Meaning: to make something bad less severe or serious.
example_sentence: Planting trees can help mitigate flooding.

title: Word: juxtapose
body: Meaning: to place two things side by side, especially to show a contrast.
example_sentence: The film juxtaposes wealth and poverty in the same street.

title: Word: ephemeral
body: Meaning: lasting for a very short time.
example_sentence: Social media fame is often ephemeral.

title: Word: diligent
body: Meaning: showing care and steady effort in your work.
example_sentence: A diligent student reviews notes every evening.

title: Word: conundrum
body: Meaning: a confusing and difficult problem or question.
example_sentence: Saving money while prices rise is a real conundrum.

title: Word: pertinent
body: Meaning: relevant to the matter being discussed.
example_sentence: Please keep your questions pertinent to today's topic.

title: Word: tenacious
body: Meaning: holding firmly to a goal; determined and persistent.
example_sentence: Her tenacious effort finally got the project funded.

title: Word: nuance
body: Meaning: a subtle difference in meaning, expression or sound.
example_sentence: A good translator understands the nuance of each word.

title: Phrase: in light of
body: Meaning: considering or because of something. Useful in formal writing.
example_sentence: In light of the new evidence, we changed our plan.

title: Phrase: by the same token
body: Meaning: for the same reason; in the same way. Use it to extend an argument.
example_sentence: Hard work brings rewards; by the same token, laziness has costs.

title: Phrase: it stands to reason
body: Meaning: it is logical or obvious.
example_sentence: If you practise daily, it stands to reason that you will improve.

title: Phrase: on balance
body: Meaning: after considering all the facts. A strong way to begin a conclusion.
example_sentence: On balance, the benefits of the plan outweigh the costs.

title: Phrase: a case in point
body: Meaning: a good example of what has just been said.
example_sentence: Some cities have cut traffic; Kigali's car-free days are a case in point.

title: Phrase: having said that
body: Meaning: despite what I have just said. Introduces a contrast politely.
example_sentence: The hotel was expensive. Having said that, the service was excellent.

title: Phrase: food for thought
body: Meaning: something worth thinking about seriously.
example_sentence: Your comments gave me a lot of food for thought.

title: Phrase: to put it another way
body: Meaning: said differently, to make something clearer.
example_sentence: We spend more than we earn. To put it another way, we are in debt.

title: What is a comma splice?
body: A comma splice joins two full sentences with only a comma. Wrong: 'I love tech, I love building.' Right: 'I love tech. I love building.' Or: 'I love tech, and I love building.' Or use a semicolon.

title: Its or it's?
body: 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has'. 'Its' shows ownership, with no apostrophe: 'The company changed its logo.' Test: if you can say 'it is', write 'it's'.

title: There, their, they're
body: 'There' is a place (over there). 'Their' shows ownership (their car). 'They're' means 'they are' (they're late). Read your sentence with 'they are' to test the third.

title: Fewer or less?
body: Use 'fewer' for things you can count: fewer cars, fewer mistakes. Use 'less' for things you measure: less water, less time. 'Fewer than 10 items', not 'less than 10 items'.

title: Affect or effect?
body: 'Affect' is usually a verb: 'Rain affects traffic.' 'Effect' is usually a noun: 'Rain has an effect on traffic.' Memory trick: Affect is the Action, Effect is the End result.

title: Subject-verb agreement
body: The verb must match the real subject, not the nearest noun. 'The list of items is long' (the list is long), not 'are long'. 'Each of the students has a book', not 'have'.

title: Parts of speech: adverbs
body: An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb. It often ends in -ly: 'She spoke clearly.' Some do not: fast, well, very, often. 'He runs fast' uses 'fast' as an adverb.

title: Active and passive voice
body: Active: the doer comes first. 'The manager approved the plan.' Passive: 'The plan was approved by the manager.' Active is usually clearer and shorter. Use passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

title: Who or whom?
body: 'Who' does the action (like he). 'Whom' receives it (like him). Test with he/him: 'Who called?' (he called). 'To whom did you write?' (you wrote to him).

title: i.e. or e.g.?
body: 'e.g.' means 'for example' (exempli gratia) and gives one or more examples. 'i.e.' means 'that is' (id est) and restates or clarifies. 'Bring fruit, e.g. apples' vs 'the capital, i.e. Nairobi'.

title: Their or they're?
body: Spot the error.
statement: 'Their going home now' is correct English
explanation: 'They're' means 'they are'. 'Their' shows ownership, as in 'their home'.

title: Fewer people
body: Countable or not?
statement: 'Fewer people came than expected' is correct
explanation: People can be counted, so 'fewer' is right. 'Less' is for amounts you measure.

title: Irregardless
body: Formal English check.
explanation: Dictionaries list 'irregardless' as nonstandard. In formal writing, use 'regardless'.

title: Spot the adverb
body: Parts of speech.
statement: In 'She sings beautifully', 'beautifully' is an adverb
explanation: 'Beautifully' describes how she sings, which is the verb, so it is an adverb.

title: Could of
body: Common mistake.
statement: 'I could of helped' is correct in formal writing
explanation: 'Could've' sounds like 'could of', but the correct form is 'could have'.

title: Between you and me
body: Pronoun check.
statement: 'Between you and I' is grammatically correct
explanation: After a preposition like 'between', use the object form: 'me', not 'I'.

title: Plural of criterion
body: Tricky plurals.
explanation: 'Criterion' comes from Greek. One criterion, two criteria. Like phenomenon and phenomena.

title: Affect or effect in use
body: Word choice.
statement: 'The new law will effect everyone' uses the right word
correct_answer: The new law will affect everyone
explanation: Here we need the verb meaning 'to influence', which is 'affect'. 'Effect' is usually the noun.
